strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practical problem: composing specialized multimodal models without additional joint training, which could improve modularity and adaptability.

The proposed system integrates a controller LLM, cross-modal memory, and parallel TTS into a coherent workflow, with some implementation details provided in the appendix (algorithm, instruction set, memory schema, and segmentation rules).
The use of explicit control tokens (e.g., [S.need_vision], [S.stop], [S.listen]) makes the orchestration process more interpretable than a purely end-to-end black-box model.
The evaluation spans multiple benchmarks (MMBench, MME, MMStar, MMMU, MathVision, CC-OCR, AI2D, InfoVQA, Video-MME) and compares against several strong baselines.
weaknesses: Central claims are not supported by controlled experiments. The system can call strong pretrained experts (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-72B, Qwen2.5-Omni, reasoning LLMs), but the paper never isolates the contribution of orchestration itself. There is no ablation showing that routing/memory/TTS improves over simply using the best single expert or a static ensemble.

Benchmark results are inconsistent and appear cherry-picked. For example, Table 2 reports Ours MME = 1922, lower than Qwen2.5-Omni (2340), Qwen-VL-Max (2281), VITA (2006.5), and Qwen2.5-VL-72B (1980), yet the text emphasizes only benchmarks where Ours leads. Table 3 also shows Ours AI2D = 78.98, far below LLaVA-OV-72B (85.60), Claude 3.5 Sonnet (94.70), and GPT-4o (94.20), which is not discussed.

The efficiency claim is misleading. The abstract and introduction claim reduced latency and significantly enhanced computational efficiency, but the measured 10.3% TTS speedup is only from 0.204s to 0.183s on a micro-component. End-to-end response time in Table 1 is 3.2s for Ours versus 1.2s for GPT-4o, so the system is not clearly more efficient. No FLOPs, GPU memory, cost, or total inference calls are reported.

The 'training-free' framing is overstated. The system still depends on large pretrained models, prompt engineering, a semantic classifier for routing, and possibly auxiliary models for memory compression. It avoids joint training but does not avoid the training cost or data requirements of the underlying models.

The cross-modal memory mechanism is underspecified. The paper claims unified storage of multimodal context and selective avoidance of modality calls, but does not explain how images/audio are represented for LLM reasoning (e.g., embeddings vs. text summaries), how retrieval is implemented, or how compression preserves fidelity. No evaluation measures memory accuracy, retrieval quality, or reduced modality calls.

Parallel TTS and full-duplex interaction claims are not evaluated. There is no measurement of time-to-first-audio, interruption latency, duplex turn-taking accuracy, speech quality (MOS), intelligibility, or prosody. The single comparison in Figure 4 is insufficient to support 'true full-duplex interaction' and 'seamless interruption handling'.

Reproducibility is poor. No code, model checkpoints, exact prompts, routing thresholds, random seeds, or compute details are provided. Some results are referenced from official papers rather than re-evaluated consistently, and the evaluation harness/protocol for Ours is not described. The claim of open-sourcing is not backed by a link or artifact.

Presentation and technical consistency are weak. There are typos and formatting errors (e.g., 'InternLM-XComposer2.5-OmniLiveand[31],M2-omni[58],LLaVA-OV' and inconsistent control tokens [Sneed_vision] vs [S.need_vision]). Table 1 mixes missing entries with strong claims, and the relationship between Table 1 and Table 2 is unclear.

Limitations and ethics are not addressed. There is no limitations section, no discussion of failure modes, privacy risks of storing multimodal user memory, consent, data security, or potential misuse. This is especially important for an interactive multimodal system with audio and visual memory.

The novelty over existing agent/tool-orchestration frameworks (e.g., AutoGen, LLaVA-Plus, mmctagent, HuggingGPT-style systems) is incremental. The contribution is primarily an engineering integration of existing components rather than a new learning method or theoretical insight.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant goal: composing specialized MLLMs without end-to-end retraining, with modularity and interpretability as explicit design targets.

The proposed architecture is clearly decomposed into a controller LLM, cross-modal memory, and parallel TTS, and the appendix provides some implementation-level details such as control tokens, a prompt template, a memory JSON schema, and TTS segmentation rules.
The reported results across several multimodal benchmarks and the TTS latency measurements suggest that training-free orchestration is a plausible engineering direction worth exploring.
The use of explicit control tokens for routing and a structured cross-modal memory is conceptually simple and potentially extensible to new modalities or expert models.
weaknesses: The central claim that training-free orchestration outperforms training-based omni-modal models is not adequately supported. The system can call multiple large expert models (Qwen2.5-VL-7B/32B/72B, Qwen-VL-Max, Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, LLaVA-Video, etc.), yet it is compared mainly against single models without compute-controlled baselines such as best-single-model, oracle routing, random routing, or simple ensembles. Gains may therefore come from using more/larger models rather than from orchestration.

The evaluation protocol is under-specified and not reproducible. There are no details on per-benchmark routing decisions, exact prompts, model versions, number of expert calls, latency measurement setup, or whether benchmark-specific hints are used. Many baseline numbers appear to be cited from official papers under different evaluation conditions, making the comparison unreliable.

Several reported results are extraordinary and unexplained. For example, MMMU 70.04 vs GPT-4o/Qwen2.5-Omni 59.20 and MMStar 69.37 vs Qwen2.5-VL-72B 68.22 are far above what the described routing among Qwen2.5-VL models would naturally suggest. No analysis identifies which expert calls produce these gains, raising concerns about leakage, cherry-picking, or inconsistent evaluation.

The abstract and contributions contain inconsistent overclaims: the abstract claims up to 7.8% improvement over jointly-trained approaches, while the contribution list mentions +1.93% on MMBench and +2.73% on AI2D. The 7.8% figure appears to refer to video improvements over a base model, not over jointly-trained omni-modal systems.

The paper claims consistent superiority, but Table 1 shows Video-MME performance of 65.58 for 'Ours' versus 71.90 for GPT-4o and 65.74 for Qwen2.5-VL-72B, and Table 3 shows AI2D 78.98 versus 94.20 for GPT-4o and 94.70 for Claude 3.5 Sonnet. These results directly contradict the broad claims of outperforming state-of-the-art models.

No component ablations are provided. There is no isolated evaluation of controller routing accuracy, cross-modal memory integration/compression, parallel TTS, or interruption handling. It is therefore impossible to attribute the reported improvements to the proposed modules rather than to the underlying expert models.

The TTS evaluation is insufficient. It reports only average processing time and variance, with no speech quality, naturalness, intelligibility, or MOS evaluation. The claimed 10.3% latency reduction is small, and the measurement setup is unclear. No human study evaluates interruption handling or full-duplex interaction.

Novelty is limited. LLM-based agent orchestration, tool routing, streaming TTS, and structured memory are well-established ideas; the paper is largely a system integration and prompt-engineering effort. The 'training-free' framing is weakened by reliance on multiple large pretrained models and by the lack of a training-free routing baseline.

Presentation and technical consistency issues hinder understanding and reproducibility. Control token notation varies between [S.need_vision], [Sneed_vision], and [S.need_*]. Algorithm 1 contains typos such as f_cbl vs. f_ctrl and token-indexing inconsistencies. The instruction set table is inconsistent with the text.

Reproducibility and research ethics are not adequately addressed. Despite mentioning open-sourcing, no code or model release is provided. There is no limitations section, no discussion of privacy risks from storing multimodal memory, no compute/cost comparison, and no discussion of licensing or API terms for commercial models used in the pipeline.

The efficiency claim is overstated. The reported response time of 3.2s is slower than GPT-4o's 1.2s, and the system depends on multiple large models and a 14B controller, so the practical computational cost is likely much higher than that of a single specialized model. No FLOPs, token usage, or monetary cost analysis is given.

The method description lacks important formal details: how the controller prompt is dynamically composed, how special control tokens are reliably parsed from free-form LLM outputs, and how routing failures are detected and handled. No error analysis of the controller is provided.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and practical problem: composing multimodal capabilities from existing specialist models without expensive joint training, which is a reasonable and potentially useful direction.

The framework is modular and its three components (controller-based routing, cross-modal JSON memory, and streaming/parallel TTS) are clearly separable, offering a plausible path to extensibility and interpretability.
The parallel-batch TTS design with semantic segmentation and streaming playback is a sensible engineering idea for reducing perceived latency in interactive systems.
The evaluation spans a broad set of benchmarks (MMBench, MMStar, MMMU, Video-MME, MathVision, CC-OCR, AI2D, InfoVQA), which is a good breadth of coverage.
weaknesses: The central quantitative claim is implausible and unexplained. The system orchestrates Qwen2.5-VL 7B/32B/72B (and others), yet 'Ours' reports MMBench-EN 88.54 and MMMU 70.04, beating the strongest constituent (72B: 86.61 and 59.20). A router that selects among experts can at best approach the oracle-best single model unless the controller adds new capability; the paper provides no mechanism (e.g., ensembling, voting, controller-side reasoning over expert outputs) and no oracle/upper-bound comparison to justify gains above the best expert.

There are no ablations. The contributions of the controller, the cross-modal memory, the reasoning model, and the parallel TTS are never isolated, so it is impossible to attribute the reported gains to any component. The memory-compression function, routing accuracy, and interpretability claims are asserted but never measured.

The efficiency claims are misleading. The advertised '10.3% latency reduction' refers only to the TTS submodule (0.204s to 0.183s), a tiny fraction of end-to-end response time, yet the abstract and contributions present it as a system-level improvement. Total inference cost (invoking a 14B controller plus multiple large VL models) is not reported, so the 'efficiency' framing is unsupported and likely unfavorable relative to single models.

The comparisons are not compute- or setup-controlled. 'Ours' aggregates many large models but is compared against single models; several baseline numbers are 'referenced from the official papers,' mixing evaluation protocols. The abstract's claim of improvement 'over traditional jointly-trained approaches' is not actually tested against a jointly-trained model of comparable scale.

Benchmark labeling and notation are inconsistent and error-prone: MMMU is described as 'temporal reasoning' (it is multi-discipline reasoning), Table 1 mislabels Video-MME under 'General Multimodal,' control tokens are written inconsistently ([S.stop] vs [S.stop], Sneed_vision vs [S.need_vision]), and the algorithm uses 'f_cbl' vs 'f_ctrl'. These signal sloppiness that undermines confidence.

Reproducibility is weak. No code/data release link is provided despite a promise to open-source; the prompt composer, lightweight semantic classifier, memory retrieval, and compression instantiation are left vague. Results are single-run without variance or significance reporting.

Originality is limited. Controller-LLM routing, structured memory, and chunked/parallel TTS are all established ideas; the contribution is largely an engineering integration rather than a new method or new understanding, and the paper does not position itself against existing orchestration/agent-routing literature beyond a brief related-work list.
